kept.a:
Domaine Weinbach’s Sylvaner is the second pour of the dinner tasting’s wine pairing, a 4 oz glass with the Tuna Crudo; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

The estate is at Kaysersberg, in the Haut-Rhin of Alsace, at the foot of the Schlossberg hill. Capuchin friars built the house and walled its vineyard, the Clos des Capucins, in 1612. After the Revolution the state sold it, and in 1898 two brothers, tanners of Kaysersberg, bought it; their family runs it still, and farms it biodynamically.

Sylvaner is an old grape of Central Europe, in Alsace an everyday white. Weinbach’s comes from old vines in the clos, on sand and silt over granite pebbles, and is made dry in large old casks: high in acidity, with pear, hay and a lemon edge. Our sheet’s words are ripe pear with green notes and a lush texture.

The sheet prints no vintage: confirm the year open before you name one.

Sell it inside the pairing as the quiet surprise: few guests have tasted Sylvaner, and a vineyard walled by friars in 1612 is a story a table remembers. Lead with dry, then the pear, then the friars. Say: “A dry Sylvaner from Domaine Weinbach in Alsace, from a monastery vineyard: ripe pear and green herbs for the tuna.” A glass outside the pairing is the sommelier’s call.

Asked: What is Sylvaner?

Answer: An old white grape of Central Europe. In Alsace it makes everyday wine, and from old vines like these a white with real texture. This one is dry.

Asked: Is it sweet, like some Alsace wines?

Answer: No. It is dry, with high acidity; the ripeness you taste is pear fruit, not sugar.

Asked: Why this with the tuna?

Answer: Its acidity meets the citrus of the aguachile, the pear sits with the carrot and the burnt orange, and its green note picks up the coriander.

The sheet of 22 November 2026 prints no vintage: never name a year until the sommelier confirms the bottle. The wine is dry, so the chili in the aguachile shows more than it would beside an off-dry Riesling; say so to a guest who is wary of heat. It replaced the Fichet Mâcon-Igé, a Chardonnay, as the second pour. It has no glass price. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Pour 4 oz as the Tuna Crudo lands, at 48 to 52°F, in a white-wine glass, label toward the guest, guests first and the host last. It is an included pour, so never top it up unasked. Say: “Sylvaner from Domaine Weinbach in Alsace: dry, ripe pear and green herbs for your tuna.” Clear the Champagne glass only when it is empty.

kept.q: Why this pour with this course?
kept.a:
The Tuna Crudo is raw tuna under a carrot and ginger aguachile, salsa seca, burnt orange, coriander, pickled pearl onions and Maldon salt: cool, sharp with citrus, gently hot and herbal. It wants a white with acidity to match the aguachile, no oak and no tannin, which turn bitter or metallic beside raw fish and chili, and no heavy alcohol, which would fan the heat.

The Sylvaner is dry and high in acidity, so it meets the citrus and the pickled onions head on. Its ripe pear sits beside the sweet carrot and the burnt orange, its green note bridges the coriander, and its lush texture holds the meaty tuna. Being dry, it lets the chili show; the off-dry Berres Riesling by the glass would cool it more.

kept.a:
The Domaine du Vieux Lazaret Blanc is the third pour of the dinner tasting’s wine pairing, a 4 oz glass with the Fish Bouillabaisse; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

Châteauneuf-du-Pape is a village and appellation of the Southern Rhône. Guests know its red; white is a small part, about 7 percent of the vines, and Grenache Blanc is its most planted white grape. The estate belongs to a family that bought its first vines in the village in 1748. Its name recalls the old lazaret, a hospice run by the Lazarists, where the sick were nursed and kept apart in the epidemics, the plague of 1720 among them; the estate has carried the name since 1915.

The white is about half Grenache Blanc, with Clairette, Bourboulenc and a little Roussanne, made almost entirely in steel or concrete tanks. Our sheet’s words: white flowers, lemon and apricot with a full-bodied texture. The sheet prints no vintage, so confirm it at lineup.

Sell it as the surprise of the pairing: a white from a village every guest knows for red. Name the village, then the body, then the story of the old plague hospice if the table enjoys one. Say: “A white Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Grenache Blanc with Clairette: white flowers, lemon and apricot, with the body for the aioli.” Ask the sommelier before offering a glass outside the pairing.

Asked: I thought Châteauneuf-du-Pape was red?

Answer: Most of it is. White is a small share of the village, about 7 percent of the vines, and this is one: Grenache Blanc with Clairette, Bourboulenc and a little Roussanne.

Asked: What does Vieux Lazaret mean?

Answer: The old lazaret: a village hospice where the sick were nursed and kept apart in the plague years. The estate has carried the name since 1915.

Asked: Is it oaked?

Answer: Mostly not. It is made in steel and concrete tanks, so the fruit and the flowers lead.

The sheet of 22 November 2026 prints no vintage, and the blend shifts a little from year to year: say Grenache Blanc leads, and never give shares or a year until the sommelier confirms the bottle. It replaced the Louis Jadot Beaune, a red, as the third pour. Serve it cool, not ice cold, or the body and the flowers close up. Allergens: read the service note and confirm at lineup.

Pour 4 oz as the Fish Bouillabaisse lands, at 50 to 54°F, in a larger white-wine glass, label toward the guest, guests first and the host last. It is an included pour, so never top it up unasked. Say: “A white Châteauneuf-du-Pape from Domaine du Vieux Lazaret, for the bouillabaisse.” Keep the open bottle cool, not buried in ice.

kept.q: Why this pour with this course?
kept.a:
The Fish Bouillabaisse is a stuffed fish terrine with a shrimp mousse, bouillabaisse sauce, chickpea panisse, confit fennel and a preserved lemon aioli: rich, garlicky, aromatic and Provençal. It wants a white with real body for the aioli and the mousse, freshness for the lemon, and no tannin, which turns metallic with fish.

This white Châteauneuf-du-Pape has the full body the sheet names, so the aioli does not flatten it. Its lemon picks up the preserved lemon, its white flowers and apricot sit with the fennel and the sauce, and Clairette and Bourboulenc keep it fresh. It is a wine of the south for a dish of Marseille. A light, crisp white would taste thin here; the Minuty rosé by the glass is the lighter choice.

entries.value: Five courses. Wine pairing supplement $120, five 4 oz pours, as the Dinner Pairing Wines sheet of 22 November 2026 lists them: Charles Lafitte Champagne with the oysters, Domaine Weinbach Sylvaner with the Tuna Crudo, Domaine du Vieux Lazaret Châteauneuf-du-Pape Blanc with the Fish Bouillabaisse, Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon with the duck and Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls with the Chocolate Crémeux. The pairing climbs from light to rich: Champagne, a dry Alsace white, a full southern white, a Napa red and a sweet fortified red. The sheet prints no vintage: confirm each bottle at lineup before you name a year. Open the Hobbs 30 to 60 minutes ahead; pour the Banyuls before the crémeux lands. Read the printed card on shift. The pairing costs more than the food; do not apologize for it.

value.q: Why this pour with this course?
value.a:
The first course is Grand Isle Jewel oysters served raw on the half shell with a preserved Fresno chili mignonette and parsley: briny, cold and sharp with vinegar, with a little heat. It wants a wine with acidity to meet the vinegar, a clean finish for the brine and no oak or tannin, which read metallic beside raw oysters.

A Brut Champagne does all of it. Its acidity answers the mignonette, its bubbles scrub the palate between oysters, and the small sweetness of a Brut softens the chili. The sheet’s crisp apple and honey sit beside the oyster’s own sweetness, and a light first pour leaves room for the four that follow.

entries.value:
Paul Hobbs Coombsville Cabernet Sauvignon is the fourth pour of the dinner tasting’s wine pairing, a 4 oz glass with the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast; it is not on the by-the-glass list.

The winery was founded in 1991 at Sebastopol, in Sonoma County, by the winemaker whose name is on the label. This Cabernet comes from Coombsville, KOOMZ-vil, just east of the city of Napa: a bowl of low hills under the Vaca Range, on volcanic soils of tuff, ash and old lava, cooled by fog and breezes off San Pablo Bay. It became its own appellation in 2011. The cool air lets the fruit ripen slowly and keep its freshness.

It is blended from the winery’s Coombsville lots, mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with a little Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot and Merlot, and aged in French oak. Our sheet gives blackberry, cassis, sage and tobacco with elegant, silky tannins.

The sheet prints no vintage; the record holds the 2021, so confirm the year at lineup. Open it 30 to 60 minutes ahead.

value.q: Why this pour with this course?
value.a:
The fourth course is Rohan duck breast, roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy, with cane syrup glazed peaches and candied hazelnuts: rich, fatty, sweet and nutty. It wants a red with dark fruit and enough tannin to bind with the fat, and the ripeness not to taste sour beside the glaze.

The Coombsville Cabernet brings blackberry and cassis for the peaches, sage and tobacco for the roasted skin, and tannins the sheet calls silky, firm enough for the fat without turning hard. The risk is the glaze: sweetness in food makes a dry red taste firmer and sharper, so the wine’s ripeness carries it. For a guest who wants it lighter, the Damien Martin Pinot Noir by the glass is the classic duck match.

entries.value: The dinner tasting’s dessert wine, the fifth course’s 4 oz pour with the Chocolate Crémeux. Our pairing sheet: “Notes of sweet jammy dark fruits and exotic spice.” A sweet, fortified red from the Collioure terraces, its Reserva aged for years partly in large casks and partly in glass jars set out in the sun, which turns it toward dried fig, walnut, caramel and coffee; the Rimage is the young, fresh black fruit style, if a guest asks. The classic wine for chocolate.

entries.value: Domaine La Tour Vieille’s Banyuls Reserva is a sweet red from the terraces of Collioure in Roussillon, mostly Grenache, its fermentation stopped with grape spirit so the grape’s own sugar stays. It ages for years partly in large casks and partly in glass jars left out in the sun. Our sheet gives sweet jammy dark fruits and exotic spice, over dried fig and caramel. Sweet enough that chocolate never turns it bitter, it closes our Dinner Tasting Menu with the Chocolate Crémeux, the cocoa nibs and the salt. We pour 4 oz, about 55°F, in a small dessert glass.

value.q: Why this pour with this course?
value.a:
The fifth course is a chocolate crémeux, a dense chocolate custard, with a cocoa nib crumble, lemon olive oil and Maldon salt: rich, deep in cocoa, a little bitter from the nibs, bright from the lemon. Chocolate turns any wine drier and more bitter than it is, so the glass must be at least as sweet as the plate and low in tannin.

Banyuls is both. Its sweetness stands up to the chocolate, its jammy dark fruit and exotic spice sit with the cocoa and the nibs, and the salt makes the chocolate taste sweeter still beside it. A dry red here would taste sour and bitter; a young Vintage Port has more grip than the crémeux wants.
